This lesson was written by the Atomic teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 4: The Structure of an Atom.
Everything in the Universe is made of particles.
Atoms are the smallest particles of an element that can exist.
The ancient Greeks called them 'atomos', meaning uncuttable.
But were they right?
Let's look inside the atom.
Think of atoms as plastic building blocks.
Each element is made of identical atoms of one type,
like one kind of block.
A hydrogen atom is like a one-stud block,
and helium is like a two-stud block.
Atoms of different elements have different sizes and masses.
And just as a few types of block can build houses,
cars and whole cities,
a small number of types of atom build everything in the Universe.
If we could open up a helium atom,
we'd find it's mostly empty space, with just three types of particle inside.
At the centre is a tiny nucleus, containing protons,
which have a positive charge, and neutrons, which have no charge.
Protons and neutrons have the same mass.
Orbiting the nucleus are electrons, with a negative charge.
They're tiny: about 1836 times lighter than a proton!
An atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons,
so the charges balance and the atom is neutral.
A balloon is rubbed on dry hair,
then held near a thin stream of water from a tap,
without touching it. Predict: what will the water do?
Pause and decide.
Watch. Rubbing moves electrons from the hair onto the balloon,
giving it a negative charge.
When the balloon comes close, the stream of water bends towards it.
Explain what you saw.
The balloon has extra electrons, so it is negatively charged.
The positive parts of the water are attracted towards it,
because opposite charges attract.
This is the same force that holds negative
electrons around the positive nucleus in an atom.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Just like magnets, like charges repel and opposite charges attract.
In an atom, the positive protons in the nucleus pull on the negative electrons.
This pull is the electrostatic force.
It acts like an invisible rope, stopping the electrons flying away.
Another force, the nuclear force, holds the protons together in the nucleus.
Try it! Rub a balloon on your hair,
and some electrons move from your hair onto the balloon,
giving it a negative charge.
Hold it near an empty can lying on its side,
and the can rolls towards it!
The atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus.
It is different for every element.
Hydrogen has 1 proton, helium 2, carbon 6, nitrogen 7,
oxygen 8 and sodium 11.
Pause and decide: a neutral sodium atom has 11 protons.
How many electrons does it have, and how are they arranged in shells?
Atoms of different elements have different numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons.
Hydrogen has 1 proton and 1 electron.
Helium has 2 protons, 2 neutrons and 2 electrons.
Carbon has 6 of each, nitrogen 7, and oxygen 8.
Electrons move in paths called shells.
The first shell holds up to 2 electrons,
and the next holds up to 8.
So carbon has 2 electrons in its inner shell and 4 in its outer shell.
The number of protons is the atomic number.
It decides which element an atom is,
and it also tells us the number of electrons.
Each element also has its own symbol: carbon is C,
but chlorine is Cl, and helium is He.
Atoms are most stable when their outer shell is full:
2 electrons in the first shell, or 8 in later shells.
A hydrogen atom has just 1 electron,
so two hydrogen atoms share their electrons, and both get a full shell.
Together they form a stable hydrogen molecule, H2.
Two nitrogen atoms share electrons in the same way to make N2.
Carbon has 4 outer electrons and needs 4 more,
so it bonds easily with other carbon atoms and other elements.
That's why carbon is the building block of living things.
Carbon atoms can have different numbers of neutrons: carbon-12 has 6,
but carbon-14 has 8.
These are called isotopes,
and carbon-14 helps scientists find the age of things that were once alive.
Sodium has 11 electrons, with just 1 in its outer shell.
That electron is held weakly, so sodium loses it easily,
which makes sodium very reactive.

captions: Atoms are far too small to see without special microscopes,
so scientists built models: simplified pictures of how atoms work.
In 1803, John Dalton imagined atoms as tiny, solid balls,
a different one for each element.
Thomson, who had discovered electrons, suggested the 'plum pudding' model:
negative electrons stuck in a positive 'soup'.
In 1911, Ernest Rutherford showed that an atom has a tiny, dense nucleus,
with electrons moving around it, like planets around the Sun.
In 1913, Niels Bohr improved this: electrons move in fixed shells.
In 1926, Erwin Schrödinger used complex mathematics to
describe electrons as a cloud around the nucleus.
And in 1932, James Chadwick discovered the neutron,
explaining the mass of the atom.
Each scientist built on the work of those before.
Rutherford fired positively charged alpha particles at a very thin sheet of gold.
In the plum pudding model, positive charge is spread thinly through the atom.
Predict: what should happen to the alpha particles?
Pause and decide.
Watch. The particles hit the gold foil,
and a screen all around records where they go.
Most particles pass straight through.
A few are deflected at large angles,
and a very few bounce straight back.
Explain what you saw.
Most particles passed straight through, so the atom must be mostly empty space.
The few that bounced back must have hit something tiny,
dense and positively charged: the nucleus.
The plum pudding model could not explain this,
so Rutherford replaced it with the nuclear model.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Now it is your turn to shine!
Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: Name the three particles in an atom and their charges.
Pause the video now.
Answer: Proton: positive · neutron: no charge · electron: negative.
Question 2: Oxygen's atomic number is 8.
How many electrons does an oxygen atom have?
Pause the video now.
Answer: 8: two in the first shell and six in the second.
Question 3: Which force holds electrons in an atom?
Pause the video now.
Answer: The electrostatic force – opposite charges attract.
Question 4: What did the gold foil experiment show?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Atoms are mostly empty space with a tiny, dense, positive nucleus.
